lessons.title: Introduction to Fractions
lessons.summary: Understand what a fraction represents and how to read numerators and denominators.
body: A fraction describes a part of a whole. It is written as one number over another, separated by a line.
The top number is the numerator. It tells you how many parts you have.
The bottom number is the denominator. It tells you how many equal parts the whole is divided into.
For example, 3/4 means you have 3 of the 4 equal parts that make up the whole.
Fractions appear everywhere: measuring ingredients, reading time, sharing money, and comparing scores.

quiz.question: In the fraction 3/4, which number is the numerator?
What does the denominator tell you?
options: How many equal parts the whole is split into
The total of numerator and denominator

quiz.question: Which fraction represents one half?

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
lessons.summary: Learn how to add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, then with different denominators.
body: When two fractions have the same denominator, you add or subtract only the numerators.
For example, 2/5 + 1/5 = 3/5. The denominator stays the same.
When denominators differ, first find a common denominator.
For 1/2 + 1/3, the common denominator is 6, so the sum becomes 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.
Always simplify your answer if the numerator and denominator share a factor.

quiz.question: What is 2/5 + 1/5?
To add 1/2 + 1/3, what common denominator do you use?
What is 3/6 + 2/6?

lessons.title: Decimals and Place Value
lessons.summary: Understand decimal notation and how place value works to the right of the decimal point.
body: A decimal point separates whole numbers from parts of a whole.
The first digit after the decimal is the tenths place, the second is the hundredths place.
So 0.5 means five tenths, and 0.25 means twenty-five hundredths.
Decimals and fractions describe the same idea — 0.5 is the same as 1/2.
Reading decimals aloud helps you keep the place values straight.

quiz.question: What does the first digit after the decimal point represent?
Which fraction equals 0.25?
0.5 is the same as which fraction?

lessons.title: Introduction to Algebra
lessons.summary: Meet variables, expressions, and simple equations — the building blocks of algebra.
body: Algebra uses letters to stand in for unknown numbers. These letters are called variables.
An expression combines numbers, variables, and operations — for example, 3x + 2.
An equation says two expressions are equal, like 3x + 2 = 11.
To solve an equation, isolate the variable by doing the same operation on both sides.
Algebra is a language for describing patterns and relationships.

quiz.question: What is a variable?
options: A letter that stands for an unknown number

quiz.question: Solve for x: x + 4 = 9
Which of these is an equation?

lessons.title: Geometry Basics: Angles and Lines
lessons.summary: Explore points, lines, angles, and how to measure them.
body: A point marks a location. A line extends infinitely in both directions.
An angle is formed where two lines meet at a point.
Angles are measured in degrees. A full circle is 360 degrees.
A right angle is exactly 90 degrees, often marked with a small square.
Angles smaller than 90 degrees are acute; larger ones up to 180 are obtuse.

quiz.question: How many degrees are in a full circle?
What is a right angle?
An angle smaller than 90 degrees is called…

lessons.title: Introduction to Cells
lessons.summary: Discover the basic unit of life — the cell — and what makes it work.
body: All living things are made of cells. Some organisms are a single cell; others have trillions.
Every cell is surrounded by a membrane that controls what enters and leaves.
Inside the cell, the nucleus contains genetic material that directs activity.
Cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance where chemical reactions happen.
Understanding cells is the foundation of biology, medicine, and genetics.

quiz.question: What is the basic unit of life?
What does the cell membrane do?
options: Controls what enters and leaves the cell

quiz.question: Where is genetic material stored in most cells?

lessons.title: Photosynthesis Explained
lessons.summary: How plants turn sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into food and oxygen.
body: Photosynthesis is the process plants use to make their own food.
Plants absorb sunlight, water from the soil, and carbon dioxide from the air.
Chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves, captures light energy.
The plant produces glucose for energy and releases oxygen as a by-product.
Almost all life on Earth depends on photosynthesis, directly or indirectly.

quiz.question: What gas do plants take in during photosynthesis?
What is the green pigment in leaves called?
What gas is released as a by-product?

lessons.title: The Human Digestive System
lessons.summary: Follow food from mouth to intestine and learn the role of each organ.
body: Digestion begins in the mouth, where chewing and saliva break food down.
The food travels down the oesophagus into the stomach.
In the stomach, acid and enzymes further break food into a liquid mixture.
The small intestine absorbs most nutrients into the bloodstream.
The large intestine absorbs water, and the remaining waste is expelled.

quiz.question: Where does digestion begin?
Which organ absorbs most nutrients?
What is the main role of the large intestine?

lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
lessons.summary: The three laws that describe how objects move and why.
body: First law: an object stays at rest or moves in a straight line unless a force acts on it.
Second law: force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma).
Third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
These laws explain everything from a rolling ball to a rocket launch.
Understanding them helps you predict how objects behave in the real world.

quiz.question: Which law says F = ma?
What does the third law state?
options: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction

quiz.question: The first law is also known as the law of…

lessons.title: Energy: Types and Transfers
lessons.summary: Explore kinetic, potential, thermal, and other forms of energy and how they change.
body: Energy is the ability to do work. It cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred.
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion; potential energy is stored energy.
Thermal energy comes from the movement of particles.
Energy transfers constantly: a falling ball converts potential into kinetic energy.
Understanding energy helps you reason about everything from machines to weather.

quiz.question: What is kinetic energy?
Can energy be created or destroyed?
A ball at the top of a hill has mostly…

lessons.title: The Water Cycle
lessons.summary: How water moves between oceans, atmosphere, and land in a continuous cycle.
body: The water cycle describes how water moves through Earth's systems.
Evaporation turns liquid water into vapour, mostly from oceans.
Condensation forms clouds when vapour cools in the atmosphere.
Precipitation returns water to the surface as rain, snow, or hail.
Runoff and groundwater flow carry water back to oceans and rivers.

quiz.question: What process turns liquid water into vapour?
What forms clouds?
Rain, snow, and hail are all forms of…

lessons.title: Reading Maps and Coordinates
lessons.summary: Learn latitude, longitude, and how to locate places on a map.
body: Maps show the world on a flat surface using a scale and a coordinate system.
Lines of latitude run east–west and measure distance north or south of the equator.
Lines of longitude run north–south and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian.
Coordinates are written as latitude first, then longitude.
0 degrees latitude is the equator; 0 degrees longitude is the prime meridian.

quiz.question: Which lines run east–west?
What is 0 degrees latitude called?
Coordinates are written as…

lessons.title: Introduction to Programming Logic
lessons.summary: Sequencing, conditions, and loops — the three core ideas behind every program.
body: Programming is giving a computer a precise list of instructions.
Sequencing means instructions run in order, one after another.
Conditions let the program choose between paths — for example, if a score is above 50, pass.
Loops repeat a set of instructions until a condition is met.
Almost every program — from a game to a spreadsheet — is built from these three ideas.

quiz.question: What does sequencing mean in programming?
Which idea lets a program choose between paths?
What is a loop used for?

lessons.title: The Internet: How Data Travels
lessons.summary: How data moves across networks using packets, IP addresses, and protocols.
body: The internet is a global network of computers that pass data to each other.
Data is broken into small units called packets before being sent.
Each packet carries the destination IP address so it can be routed.
Protocols like TCP and IP make sure packets arrive correctly and in order.
Because packets can take different routes, the internet stays resilient.

quiz.question: What is data broken into before being sent?
What do packets carry so they can be routed?
What do TCP and IP do?
options: Ensure packets arrive correctly and in order

lessons.title: Study Skills: How to Learn Better
lessons.summary: Practical techniques to make revision more effective and less stressful.
body: Learning is a skill you can improve — it is not fixed.
Space your study across days instead of cramming it all at once.
Test yourself often. Retrieval practice beats re-reading.
Explain ideas in your own words to check understanding.
Sleep, breaks, and hydration all affect how well you learn.

quiz.question: Which technique is more effective than re-reading?
Spacing your study across days is called…
Which of these helps learning?
